🤿 Deep dive · Lesson 8 · 2 min read

Learning by Trial and Error

How an AI learns from rewards, the way you learn a new game: try, fail, try again.

Agent, environment, reward

Think of teaching a dog a trick. It tries different things, and when it sits, it gets a treat. Soon it sits when you ask. Reinforcement learning works the same way. An agent (the learner: a game character, a robot, a program) acts in an environment (the game, the room). After its actions it gets a reward: a number that says how well it did, like points in a game. Nobody shows it the right moves. It has to find out which actions bring the most reward over time.

Did you know? A video game is a perfect environment: the agent is the player, the actions are the buttons, and the reward is the score. Researchers have trained agents to play dozens of classic Atari games using nothing but the pixels on the screen and the score.

Try something new, or stick with what works?

Imagine choosing where to eat after school. You know one café is good. Do you go there again, or try the new place that might be even better? Using what you already know is exploitation; trying something new to learn more is exploration. An agent that only exploits can get stuck with “good enough”; one that only explores never uses what it has learned. A simple recipe: explore a small part of the time (say, 1 time in 10) and pick the best-known choice the rest of the time. Video and music apps face the same choice: more of what you like, or something new you might love?

Learning what each move is worth

As it plays, the agent keeps a score for every action in every situation: how much reward it expects if it does this here, counting what comes after too. These scores are often called Q-values. At first they are guesses. After each try, the agent nudges the score a little towards what actually happened. Slowly the good moves get high scores, and the agent starts to plan ahead: a move with no reward right now can still be great if it leads to a big reward later.

Did you know? When there are too many situations to list them all (think of every possible screen in a video game), the agent uses a neural network to estimate the scores instead of a table. This is called deep reinforcement learning.

Where it works, and how it goes wrong

In 2016, DeepMind's AlphaGo, which learned partly by playing millions of games against itself, beat Lee Sedol, one of the best Go players in the world. Reinforcement learning also helps robots learn to walk and grasp things. Chatbots are polished with human feedback too: people compare answers, and the model is rewarded for the kind of answers people preferred (RLHF). But an agent chases the reward, not what you meant. If the reward has a loophole, the agent may find it: that's called reward hacking.

Did you know? In 2016, OpenAI trained an agent on a boat-racing game, CoastRunners, where points came from hitting targets along the course. The agent found a lagoon where it could go round in circles, hitting the same targets again and again as they reappeared. It never finished the race, yet it scored more points than human players.

Key points

  • In reinforcement learning, an agent learns by trial and error from rewards, not from correct answers.
  • It must balance exploration (trying new actions) and exploitation (using what works).
  • An agent chases the reward it gets, so a badly designed reward can be “hacked”.

Check yourself

A robot vacuum gets a reward for every bit of dust it picks up. It starts tipping dust out and sucking it up again. What is going on?

Show the answer

Right answer: Reward hacking: it found a loophole in its reward

The robot does exactly what the reward pays for (picking up dust), not what people meant (a clean room): that's reward hacking. It isn't exploration, because it keeps repeating a trick it already knows. And nothing is broken: its sensor sees the dust perfectly well. A reward for a clean floor would be harder to trick.
